solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Not having object in van gets one very embarrassed at first

parts.note: the Ford Transit is a well-known van
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone sitting in a van is mortified at being caught there without any purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' takes just the E of 'embarrassed'. The Ford Transit is a common British van.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar term: a verb that takes no direct object, such as 'sleep', is described this way.

clue.text: Brother may be so suitable

definitions.meaning: a monk or friar belongs to a religious order, so he is a member of one
proper, fitting, as in 'that is quite correct and allowed'

explanation.surface: A sibling might be described as fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A friar is a member of a religious order, and the everyday phrase means proper or appropriate.

clue.text: Dodgy arrest right away starts to implicate PC Plod

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are put into a crooked new order
right away says the letter for right is removed from the word before
starts to takes the opening letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A dubious arrest leads a bumbling British policeman (PC Plod) to accuse someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' removes an R from ARREST, leaving AREST; 'starts to' adds I and P, and 'Dodgy' shuffles all seven. PC Plod is a comic name for a British police constable.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe walking wearily and heavily, trudging along.

clue.text: Classical writer's character that's old, extremely hearty and mostly drunk

parts.note: aesc (ash) is an Old English runic letter, written as the ligature ae

indicators.note: extremely takes the two outside letters of the word that follows
mostly removes the final letter of the synonym

parts.note: a lush is a heavy drinker, so drunk as a noun

explanation.surface: A classical author's personality is ancient, very jovial and usually tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'writer's' stands for 'is'. 'extremely' gives HY; 'mostly' trims LUSH to LUS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian tragedian, author of the Oresteia, is a classic Greek playwright.

clue.text: This tennis player's form can be up and down

indicators.note: in a down entry the name reads identically going up as going down

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A tennis player's form fluctuates, good one day and poor the next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' points to the shape of the name itself, which reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Monica Seles was a world number one women's tennis champion of the 1990s.

clue.text: Showing disapproval, for the whole band's no good

parts.note: tutti is the musical direction for all the players together

explanation.surface: Someone frowns because the whole orchestra is playing badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a clicking 'tsk' sound with the tongue expresses mild disapproval.

clue.text: To clean motor, sailor docked in island capital

parts.note: to valet a car is to clean it thoroughly

indicators.note: docked means having its tail cut off, so the last letter goes

parts.note: tar is a traditional word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor in port cleans a car in the harbour of a Mediterranean capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' cuts TAR to TA. The capital of Malta is more often spelt Valletta.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief city of Malta, an island state, in a variant spelling.

clue.text: Couturier's job is hard to quit

definitions.meaning: a dressmaker's work is making clothes, which jokingly includes nuns' or riding garments
addictive, describing something difficult to give up

explanation.surface: A fashion designer's work is something one cannot easily give up.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a garment, so a couturier shapes one; the phrase also means addictive.

clue.text: Article's a classic, capturing ultimate character of computer geeks

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: capturing means one piece is held inside another

parts.note: the Oaks is one of the five English Classic horse races

indicators.note: ultimate character of picks the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A well-known essay captures the essential nature of computer nerds.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oaks, run at Epsom, is one of Britain's five Classic flat races; it takes in the R that ends 'computer'.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for obsessive enthusiasts or nerds, from the waterproof jackets associated with trainspotters.

clue.text: Making good time, fielder didn't get to catch

indicators.note: making good into time says the letter for good becomes the letter for time

parts.note: leg slip is a cricket fielding position near the batsman

explanation.surface: A fast-moving fielder failed to reach the ball in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making good time' means G (good) is made into T (time). Leg slip is a close catching position in cricket, behind the batsman on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for allowing something to escape your grasp, as a fielder does with a dropped ball or a missed chance.

clue.text: Fireman perhaps needs a little money for something to eat

parts.note: a fireman works a fire engine's pump, so could be called one who pumps
a nickel is a US five-cent coin

explanation.surface: A firefighter wants some cash to buy a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' shows the fireman is just an example of one who pumps.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark German rye bread, so certainly an item of food.

clue.text: Vaguely hint about leader in private education turning comprehensive

indicators.note: about means going around the other piece
vaguely suggests the letters are loosely arranged in a new order
turning means the pieces it governs are read backwards
leader in takes the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone hints that private schooling is becoming comprehensive, a swipe at British state secondary schools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vaguely' rearranges the hint letters; 'turning' reverses the P and ED; 'about' wraps the shuffled letters round them. 'comprehensive' looks like the British state school but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorough and detailed, covering everything, as in a detailed study.

clue.text: Dash it, timber is partly made of wood!

indicators.note: partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An exasperated carpenter swears that the thing is partly wooden.
explanation.walkthrough: The mild oath and exclamation mark lead away from the Biblical acacia wood hidden in 'daSH IT TIMber'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical acacia wood of the Ark of the Covenant, so things made from it are of wood.

clue.text: Reportedly hides in shrub

indicators.note: reportedly says the word is to be taken as heard rather than as written

parts.note: furs are animal skins or hides

explanation.surface: Someone is said to be hiding in a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hides' looks like a verb but is the noun, animal pelts.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorse, a spiny yellow-flowered bush of heathland, goes by this other name.

clue.text: No burial at sea for German nobleman?

definitions.text: No burial at sea for German nobleman?

parts.words: No burial at sea for German nobleman?
parts.note: a grave on dry ground rather than in the ocean, read as the title of a German count

explanation.surface: A German aristocrat is spared a funeral at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the title into two words: a burial not at sea would be on land, in a grave.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval German count with jurisdiction over a territory bore this title.

clue.text: One has no need to pick up the tab

definitions.text: One has no need to pick up the tab

parts.words: One has no need to pick up the tab
parts.note: tab is slang for a cigarette, so someone who never lights one has no reason to take one

explanation.surface: Someone is excused from paying the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tab' reads as a bill but is British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who does not use cigarettes never needs to take one.

clue.text: Displaced Rentokil, oddly, as top eliminator of pests

indicators.note: displaced means moved out of place, so the letters are rearranged
oddly takes the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Rentokil, a British pest-control firm, has been ousted as the leading exterminator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes RNOI from Rentokil; with AS and TOP, 'Displaced' shuffles all nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A poison put down for rodents kills off vermin.

clue.text: Row about parking on street? He'll give better advice

indicators.note: about means going around the other pieces

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats

indicators.note: in a down clue, on puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: P is the map symbol for parking

explanation.surface: An argument over parking on a road, with someone offering sensible advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel but means a line, and 'better' is one who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing pundit gives recommendations to punters, who are gamblers on horses.

clue.text: Ham and eggs to absorb half of beer before court

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the second
to absorb means one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: ova are eggs, the plural of ovum

indicators.note: half of takes two of the four letters of the word that follows, here the back pair

explanation.surface: A breakfast of ham and eggs soaks up some beer before a court appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' is the verb, to perform too theatrically, not the meat beside the eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham it up is to exaggerate a performance theatrically.

clue.text: One's incredibly minute, for a start

definitions.text: One's incredibly minute, for a start

indicators.note: for a start takes the first letter of the word before it
incredibly suggests the letters are shaken into an unbelievable new order

parts.note: the four letters of the clue word including the s

explanation.surface: Something is unbelievably tiny, to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the particle is indeed incredibly minute.
explanation.definitionFit: A subatomic particle made of a quark and an antiquark, so tiny beyond belief.

clue.text: Rodent problem arising before otter briefly turned up

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the second
arising in a down clue means reading upwards

parts.note: a sum is a problem in arithmetic

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means written bottom to top
briefly cuts off the last letter

parts.note: Tarka is the otter of Henry Williamson's novel Tarka the Otter

explanation.surface: A rodent infestation arises before a shortened otter appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arising' turns SUM to MUS; 'briefly' trims TARKA to TARK and 'turned up' makes it KRAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A large North American aquatic rodent valued for its fur.

clue.text: Senior Tory finally admits one's out of touch, perhaps

indicators.note: admits means letting another piece inside
finally takes the last letter of the word before it
out signals the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A senior Conservative at last confesses to being out of touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' shuffles the letters of 'one's' to ENSO, which 'admits' places between S and R. 'out of touch' reads as one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Touch is one of the five senses, so pertaining to it is an example.

clue.text: Strike force to join navy?

definitions.meaning: to stamp or imprint a mark on something
to press-gang men into naval service

explanation.surface: A walkout by workers compelled to enlist with the fleet.
explanation.definitionFit: To stamp a design is one sense; the other is the historic forcible recruitment of sailors.

clue.text: Team's backed to get boundaries in Twenty Twenty and double score

indicators.note: backed in a down clue means read from the bottom upward

parts.note: a cricket or football team is an eleven, XI, so the plural is XIS

indicators.note: boundaries in takes the outside letters of the next word

explanation.surface: Cricket sides are backed to hit fours and sixes in a Twenty20 match and double their total.
explanation.walkthrough: Twenty Twenty is short-form cricket, where boundaries are fours and sixes; 'boundaries in' takes T and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so twice that is the number meant.

clue.text: Person in charge conceals note relating to secret order

indicators.note: conceals means holding another piece inside

parts.note: a man is a person
so is the fifth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: The boss hides a message concerning a covert organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person in charge' looks like one phrase for a boss but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasons form a fraternity famed for secret rites, and this adjective describes them.

clue.text: Goodies originally fed to the French?

definitions.text: Goodies originally fed to the French?

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: ate means fed, as in dined
aux is French for to the, before a plural

explanation.surface: Treats perhaps first given to the people of France.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: rich cakes are goodies fed to the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Rich layered cakes are treats, and the French word's plural form is used here.

clue.text: Kelvin, a debauched fellow, harbours love for pub entertainment

parts.note: K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature

indicators.note: harbours means sheltering another piece inside

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute man
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A man named Kelvin, a dissolute type, nurses a passion for nights out at the local.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing along to recorded backing tracks is a popular bar pastime.

clue.text: Extremely cute but heartless little child hides in quarry repeatedly

indicators.note: repeatedly says the whole construction is made twice over
hides in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: prey is a hunted animal, a quarry

indicators.note: heartless takes out the middle letter

parts.note: a tot is a little child

explanation.surface: A sweet but cruel kid hides in a gravel pit again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' leaves TT; 'repeatedly' doubles the whole. 'quarry' suggests a pit but means hunted game.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubling an adjective intensifies it; this one means excessively or cloyingly sweet-looking.
